source: Xie, Raghunathan, Liang, Ma (2022) An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference
finding: Theory: a pretrained LM infers a latent concept from the prompt and predicts under that concept. This is posterior inference, so code length under the mixture equals log-probability under the Bayes prior.
numbers: Tested on synthetic GINC (HMM mixture). In-context accuracy rises with number of examples n and example length k for Transformers and LSTMs, vocab sizes 50/100/150.
limits: Synthetic data only. The theory needs a distinguishability condition between concepts. Real LLM pretraining data is not a clean concept mixture.
agent_relevance: Gives the bridge: a prompt acts like data under a prior over tasks, so choosing between hypotheses with a prior is what the model already approximates.

source: Xie et al. (2022) ICL as Implicit Bayesian Inference (GINC scale and ordering results)
finding: On GINC, bigger models give better in-context accuracy even at the same pretraining loss. Order of examples changes accuracy a lot. Zero-shot can beat few-shot in some settings. All three mirror GPT-3 reports.
numbers: 12 vs 16 layer Transformers both reach validation loss 1.33 (vocab 50), yet in-context accuracy goes 81% to 85%. Accuracy varies widely across permutations of the same examples.
limits: Order sensitivity is already a hint that behaviour is not exact Bayes (see Falck et al.). Synthetic setting.
agent_relevance: Warns that the same evidence in a different order gives a different posterior; an agent should shuffle or average over orderings when it needs a stable choice.

source: Falck, Wang, Holmes (2024) Is In-Context Learning in LLMs Bayesian? A Martingale Perspective (ICML)
finding: Exact Bayesian prediction on exchangeable data must satisfy the martingale property. The authors test it on GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B and find violations, so ICL is not exactly Bayesian.
numbers: Bernoulli task, n=50 observed, imputed path length m=n/2: most LLMs inside the Bayesian 95% bootstrap interval (main exception GPT-4 at mean 0.3 and 0.5). m=2n: more frequent deviations. Gaussian task (n=100, m=50): all except GPT-3.5 clearly deviate. Natural-language version (n=80, m=40): GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 deviate.
quote: falsifying the hypothesis that ICL is Bayesian
limits: Small synthetic exchangeable tasks. Instruction-tuned models did not do better than GPT-3 base. Tests a necessary condition only.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the model's stated or implied belief updates are coherent. Long chains of self-imputed steps drift; a scaffold should anchor to observed data, not to imagined continuations.

source: Falck, Wang, Holmes (2024) Martingale Perspective (uncertainty scaling, T3 statistic)
finding: Epistemic uncertainty of LLMs does not shrink with more data like a Bayesian model. Llama-2-7B and GPT-3.5 shrink more slowly than Bayes. GPT-3.5 is overconfident with few samples. GPT-3 and Mistral-7B are closest to Bayes.
numbers: Bernoulli mean 0.5, n from 20 to 400, compared with a reference Bayes model and fractional-Bayes (alpha 0.5 and 2) posteriors.
limits: Only Bernoulli mean 0.5 case where all models pass the short-horizon check. Order-of-magnitude comparison only.
agent_relevance: Confidence from the model after seeing more examples is not a reliable posterior width. Calibrate externally (see the calibration subfield).

source: Arora, Jurafsky, Potts, Goodman (2025) Bayesian scaling laws for in-context learning
finding: A scaling law built straight from Bayes' theorem (prior over tasks, posterior grows with shots) fits ICL curves as well as free power laws and extrapolates best from the first 5% of the curve. Its parameters are readable as task prior and learning efficiency.
numbers: GPT-2 on GINC, normalised RMSE: Bayesian interpolation 0.0279 vs logistic 0.0268 (lowest); extrapolation from first 5% of curve: Bayesian 0.0493 vs logistic 0.1138, bounded power 0.0814 (read from table; row order partly inferred). SFT: Bayes 0.0704 vs logistic 0.0684. DPO: 0.0852 vs 0.0834. Most baseline gaps not significant (paired t-test p<0.05).
limits: Synthetic GINC plus a few real benchmarks. Bayesian law is not best at interpolation. Several comparisons not statistically significant.
agent_relevance: Supports modelling the number of examples needed as a prior-times-likelihood quantity: a strong prior on the right task means few shots suffice; a low prior means many.

source: Arora et al. (2025) Bayesian scaling laws (post-training changes the prior, not the knowledge)
finding: SFT and DPO mostly shift the fitted prior over tasks, not the per-task likelihood. On Llama 3.1 8B, instruction tuning lowers the prior on unsafe behaviours but many-shot jailbreaking still brings them back, because the posterior saturates.
numbers: 50 many-shot prompts per dataset and model, built from HarmBench plus 3 persona evals and benchmarks. In SFT, the prior shifts slowly for larger models.
quote: instruction-tuning merely modifies the prior over tasks and not task knowledge
limits: Interpretation depends on the fit being a true Bayesian mechanism. Low-data post-training in synthetic runs. Authors note post-training compute is small versus pretraining.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that only sets a prior (system prompt, persona) can be overridden by enough contrary evidence. Priors in prompts are cheap but weak against data.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen, van Steenkiste (2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs stop improving after the first round of a 5-round flight-preference task, far below a Bayesian Assistant. Fine-tuning on the Bayesian Assistant's own (often wrong early) guesses works better than fine-tuning on oracle-correct answers.
numbers: Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B. Original Gemma accuracy 37% at round 1 and round 5. Bayesian-tuned models agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time. Bayesian teaching beats oracle teaching, all p<0.001, 3 seeds. 10 five-round interactions per user for training data. Hundreds of human participants (about 720 and 500 in two studies) also tested.
limits: Narrow synthetic task with a fixed hypothesis space; uniform prior (other priors similar). Gap to the Bayesian Assistant remains.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that models do not update beliefs optimally by default and that imitating a normative Bayes procedure transfers. Also supports an explicit hypothesis-weight tracker instead of trusting free-form updating.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian Teaching (generalisation and verbal beliefs)
finding: Skill learned on flights transfers to different feature counts, hotel recommendation and a web-shopping task with real products. Original models show no sensitivity to how informative a choice set is; tuned ones do.
numbers: Fine-tuned models generalise beyond training task (Fig 5); Gemma Bayesian more sensitive to option-set informativity than Gemma Oracle. Verbalised belief ratings from untuned LLMs had under 50% alignment with beliefs implied by their choices.
limits: Transfer tested on related preference-learning tasks. Different Qwen family effect in an appendix analysis.
agent_relevance: Stated beliefs and used beliefs disagree. Make the agent record hypothesis weights explicitly rather than reading them off its prose.

source: Mueller, Hollmann, Arango, Grabocka, Hutter (2022) Transformers Can Do Bayesian Inference (PFNs, ICLR)
finding: Train a transformer on tasks sampled from a prior; it then outputs the posterior predictive in one forward pass. It near-perfectly mimics a Gaussian process and approximates intractable Bayesian neural nets.
numbers: Over 200-fold speedups on several setups versus current methods (MCMC/SVI). Tested on GP regression, BNNs, small tabular classification, few-shot image classification.
limits: Needs ability to sample from the prior. Quality depends on prior coverage and training budget; small data sizes.
agent_relevance: This is the cleanest machine case where prior choice fully determines the output: change the prior, change the posterior. Shows the prior is a design input, not a hidden constant.

source: Grau-Moya, Genewein, Hutter, Orseau, et al. (2024) Learning Universal Predictors
finding: Meta-train LSTMs and Transformers on data from random Universal Turing Machine programs to approximate Solomonoff induction, whose prior is 2^-length. Larger models predict better, and large Transformers transfer to other tasks.
numbers: On variable-order Markov sources, large LSTMs and Transformers reach cumulative regret close to the Bayes-optimal Context Tree Weighting predictor (256-step sequences, tree depth up to 24, 6k test sequences, 3 seeds); regret falls from size S to M to L.
limits: Short sequences, small alphabets. CTW is optimal only for Markov sources, not for all computable ones. Approximation of a length-prior, not the incomputable ideal.
agent_relevance: Direct machine version of 'short program means high prior probability'. Supports using description length as the prior over candidate explanations.

source: Zhang, Zhang, Yang, Wang (2023) What and How does In-Context Learning Learn? Bayesian Model Averaging
finding: Proves that ICL implicitly performs Bayesian model averaging (not picking one best model), implemented approximately by attention, with O(1/T) online regret for a perfectly pretrained model.
numbers: Regret O(1/T) with T prompt examples. Pretraining error bound = approximation error that decays exponentially with depth + generalisation error that decays sublinearly with tokens.
limits: Theory under a latent-variable data model; assumes perfect pretraining for the regret bound.
agent_relevance: Averaging over hypotheses is the Bayes route; picking the single shortest description is the MDL route. The two diverge when evidence is thin, so an agent that must commit should know which it is doing.

source: Chlon et al. (2026) LLMs are Bayesian in Expectation, Not Realization
finding: Reconciles Falck et al.: order sensitivity breaks exact exchangeability but costs only a measurable amount of log loss. Excess prequential code length equals cumulative predictive KL to the Bayes reference. Order-averaging over serialisations gives a gain.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B / 14B, support 256: one-step excess code length 0.020 / 0.011 bits (Bernoulli) and 0.039 / 0.022 bits (four-way categorical), candidate mass above 0.999. Predictions sit closer to Bayes posterior predictive than to ML plug-in, most at small support.
quote: Exchangeability violations are therefore not binary refutations; they are priced by log loss.
limits: Small synthetic prediction tasks on two Qwen sizes; instruct models. Order effect localised to positional encoding.
agent_relevance: Gives a way to measure how Bayesian the model is in bits. Averaging the answer over several example orders is the cheap fix.

source: Lotfi, Izmailov, Benton, Goldblum, Wilson (2022/2023) Bayesian Model Selection, the Marginal Likelihood, and Generalization (JMLR)
finding: The marginal likelihood (Bayes evidence, the Bayes twin of the MDL code length) tests whether a prior fits, but it can be negatively correlated with generalisation and can cause both under- and over-fitting in hyperparameter learning. Conditional marginal likelihood (score only the later data points) tracks generalisation better.
numbers: Neural hyperparameter search on CIFAR-100: correlation of Laplace BMA test accuracy with the marginal likelihood depends strongly on prior precision (values 1e2, 1e-1, 1e-3 tested); correlation with the conditional version is consistently positive.
limits: Mostly image models and Gaussian processes. Authors say marginal likelihood is fine for prior hypothesis testing, bad as a proxy for predicting trained-model accuracy.
agent_relevance: Choosing a hypothesis by total compression of all data punishes hypotheses for their early mistakes. For picking what will predict new items, score on held-back or later items.

source: Lotfi, Finzi, Kuang, Rudner, Goldblum, Wilson (2024) Non-Vacuous Generalization Bounds for Large Language Models (ICML)
finding: First non-vacuous compression-based (PAC-Bayes, MDL-style) generalisation bounds for LLMs, up to about 849M parameters, using SubLoRA to shrink the model code. Larger models have tighter bounds because they compress better.
numbers: GPT-2 small (124M), document-level bounds: SubLoRA 12.12 bits per dimension, 96.41% Top-1 error, 58.34% Top-100 error; LoRA only 13.09 BPD; original model 70.76 BPD; random guess 15.62 BPD. 354M model 11.96 BPD; 849M 12.01. Subsampled bound computation 900x faster on OpenWebText (over 9B tokens).
limits: Bounds are loose in absolute terms (Top-1 error bound 96%). Models pretrained from scratch under compression constraints.
agent_relevance: Shows that the code-length view of generalisation can be computed for real LLMs. Model complexity is paid for in bits, which is the Occam trade in a number.

source: Gruenwald and Roos (2019) Minimum Description Length Revisited (International Journal of Mathematics for Industry)
finding: Bayes marginal, two-part, NML and prequential plug-in codes are all 'universal' codes. NML minimises worst-case regret, which a Bayes mixture does not in general. Bernoulli NML complexity is within a constant of the Bayes-with-Jeffreys-prior value.
numbers: Bernoulli: NML complexity is (1/2) log n plus a constant, matching Bayes with Jeffreys prior asymptotically. Original (flat) NML integral is ill-defined for just about every model on unbounded outcome spaces such as the normal location family; luckiness functions are the fix.
limits: Theory review. Asymptotic equivalence holds for regular models; differs for small n and for unbounded spaces.
agent_relevance: For the agent: a Bayes prior rewards the favoured hypotheses; NML does not favour any. No LLM study I found uses NML; the 'no Bayes counterpart' part of the claim is untested in machines.

source: Gruenwald and Langford (2004/2007) Suboptimal Behavior of Bayes and MDL in Classification under Misspecification
finding: Constructs a learning problem where the Bayes posterior classifier and a two-part MDL classifier stay bounded away from the best achievable error at every sample size. Misspecification (true rule not in the class) breaks the usual guarantees.
numbers: No empirical sample: a proof plus constructed counterexample. Applies to Bayes on classifiers turned into likelihoods via a prior on error rates, and to two-part MDL.
limits: Authors warn it covers only some versions of Bayes and MDL. Contrived but valid counterexample.
agent_relevance: When all candidate hypotheses are wrong (very common for an LLM hypothesis list) both prior-weighted selection and shortest-description selection can stay wrong however much data arrives.

source: Gruenwald and van Ommen (2017) Inconsistency of Bayesian Inference for Misspecified Linear Models, and a Proposal for Repairing It (Bayesian Analysis)
finding: Under misspecification (data heteroskedastic, model homoskedastic) the Bayes posterior puts mass on ever higher-dimensional models as n grows. SafeBayes, which tempers the likelihood with a learning rate chosen from data, repairs it.
numbers: Simulated polynomial regression: full Bayes squared-error risk stays poor over a very large range of sample sizes; SafeBayes tends to pick small learning rates when the posterior is not cumulatively concentrated.
limits: Simulation on linear models; repair has no proof of general optimality.
agent_relevance: A tempered prior (weaker trust in each piece of evidence) is a practical guard when the hypothesis family is known to be imperfect. Equivalent in an agent to not over-updating on each observation.

source: Vitanyi and Li (2000) Minimum Description Length Induction, Bayesianism, and Kolmogorov Complexity (IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory)
finding: Ideal MDL is Bayes' rule with the algorithmic universal prior, so minimising 'length of model plus length of data given model' is the Bayes mode. Valid when data are random relative to each hypothesis and hypotheses are random relative to the prior (Fundamental Inequality).
numbers: Theorem-level; no sample. For finite-set models it reduces to Kolmogorov's minimal sufficient statistic.
quote: data compression is almost always the best strategy
limits: Uses incomputable Kolmogorov complexity; practical MDL codes are approximations and depend on the chosen coding language.
agent_relevance: Justifies using the length of a written explanation as a stand-in for its prior probability, with the caveat that the description language is the prior.

source: Gandhi, Li, Goodyear, Bhatia, Goodman et al. (2025) BoxingGym: Benchmarking Progress in Automated Experimental Design and Model Discovery
finding: LLM scientist agents propose models and choose experiments in 10 probabilistic environments. Giving the model domain context (a prior) often did not help and sometimes hurt after 10 experiments. Larger models beat smaller. Instruction-tuned beat reasoning-tuned OpenThinker.
numbers: 10 environments, 5 independent trials, 6 LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-sonnet, Qwen-2.5-32B/7B, OpenThinker-32B/7B). Test at 0,1,3,5,7,10 observations. Measures: standardised prediction error and expected information gain (EIG) regret versus 100 random experiments. GPT-4o had the lowest EIG regret. Hyperbolic discounting error increased with more observations.
limits: Benchmark; no single headline percent. Hyperbolic discounting environment hard for all models.
agent_relevance: Domain priors in the prompt can lock the model into an early wrong assumption it does not revise. Prior strength should be tested, not assumed to help.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym (Box's Apprentice, explicit probabilistic programs)
finding: Letting the LLM write and fit a PyMC model (an explicit Bayesian model) did not consistently beat plain GPT-4o. The apprentice tended to choose overly simple forms such as linear fits with little data.
numbers: Apprentice writes a PyMC program after 10 experiments, which is fit and handed to the explaining agent. Novice agent (GPT-4o) predicts from the scientist's written explanation; error compared across scientist models.
limits: Only one apprentice design; the simplicity bias may reflect prompting rather than a Bayes flaw.
agent_relevance: An MDL-like preference for simple models shows up in practice as underfitting when data is thin. Complexity penalties need a floor.

source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) In-Context Learning and Occam's Razor (already covered in 03_statistical_mdl, cited here for the Bayes link)
finding: Prequential code length of in-context learning equals a joint cost of model complexity plus training error, so next-token training on varied tasks pushes toward simple models. This is the same sum as the Bayes marginal likelihood.
numbers: See evidence_c.jsonl in subfield 03 for details (not re-opened here).
limits: Not re-read in this session. Listed only for the Bayes link.
agent_relevance: Prequential code length is the point where MDL and Bayes agree exactly for a Bayes mixture.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression (already covered in 03_statistical_mdl)
finding: Any probabilistic LM is a lossless compressor through arithmetic coding, which makes code length equal negative log probability by construction.
numbers: Not re-opened here; numbers recorded in subfield 03.
limits: Not re-read in this session.
agent_relevance: Literal 'code length matches probability' for LLMs: a candidate's log-probability under the model is its description length.

source: Blier and Ollivier (2018) The Description Length of Deep Learning Models (already covered in 03_statistical_mdl)
finding: Prequential (online) code length is a practical, non-Bayes-mixture way to score deep models; it is a sequential plug-in code, one of the four universal codes in Gruenwald and Roos.
numbers: Not re-opened here.
limits: Not re-read in this session.
agent_relevance: The prequential score works with an LLM scoring each new item after seeing the earlier ones.

source: Gap note from this search (no source): NML in LLM work
finding: In the sources opened this session I found no LLM or agent study that uses normalised maximum likelihood codes or compares NML against a Bayes mixture. The machine literature is all on Bayes, prequential or two-part codes.
numbers: Searches limited: arXiv export API and Semantic Scholar rate-limited (HTTP 429); OpenAlex calls returned errors. About 15 papers opened by direct PDF.
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search, not a proof of absence.
agent_relevance: The claim that NML has no Bayes counterpart is a theory result with no machine test; do not build the agent on it.

source: Gruenwald and Roos (2019) Minimum Description Length Revisited (prequential and sequential codes)
finding: MDL model selection can use a choice of codes that all give log-loss regret about (k/2) log n for k parameters. A Bayes marginal with any reasonable prior, plain NML and prequential plug-in agree to leading order; they differ in constants and in which hypotheses they favour.
numbers: Regret order (k/2) log n for regular parametric models (stated in the review).
limits: Leading-order equivalence, differences matter at small n, which is the usual regime for an LLM agent.
agent_relevance: With few observations, the choice of prior or code can decide which hypothesis wins. Report the margin, not only the winner.

source: Arora et al. (2025) Bayesian scaling laws (ICL efficiency K)
finding: Adds a learned efficiency coefficient K multiplying the shot count, because each example is several tokens and not equally informative. Longer, more informative examples give larger K and faster posterior concentration.
numbers: Law: posterior = sum over tasks of prior times (per-example probability)^(K n). Tying parameters cuts latent terms from M squared + M to 3M, so the law has 3M+1 parameters, same size as the power law.
limits: Fit on synthetic GINC with known ground-truth priors; priors came out roughly uniform and noisy.
agent_relevance: Quality of examples, not just count, sets how fast the model commits. Curate informative examples.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian Teaching (what the Bayesian Assistant does)
finding: The symbolic Bayesian Assistant keeps a posterior over a user's preference weights, picks the maximum-expected option, and updates after each choice. It is the teacher, not an LLM. Training on its early-round mistakes beats training on correct answers.
numbers: Uniform prior; other priors in an appendix performed similarly. DPO and LoRA gave similar results to full fine-tuning.
limits: Hypothesis space is small and exactly enumerable.
agent_relevance: This is a template for putting a normative Bayes updater beside an LLM: the LLM proposes, the tracker keeps explicit weights.

source: Falck et al. (2024) Martingale Perspective (practical implication)
finding: Authors note the violation matters for LLM-based tabular prediction and synthetic data imputation, and suggest fine-tuning towards Bayesian behaviour before deployment. They suggest similar drift may occur in chain-of-thought.
numbers: No new numbers; discussion section.
limits: Chain-of-thought link is a conjecture in the paper, not tested.
agent_relevance: Untested but plausible: long reasoning chains that impute their own premises can drift from the posterior.
